Q: How do I fix the jupyter notebook search box error "TypeError: can't access property "length", child is undefined"? A:

Fix: cut and paste the bad markup cell

There is such an easy fix to this that I had to share this. I came to think of fixing this only after many of these error messages since the notebook is huge, and I could not spend the time on it. But when I found a white space in a cell, it was too likely linked to this bug.

In short: this happens if you deal with special signs in markup cells. It happened a dozen times and always just in the markdown cells, for example:

  • after pasting from the chatbot,
  • and shortly after search-replacing a word with a new word over the whole notebook, and that new word had an umlaut "ä" in it,
  • after replacing an umlaut word with a non-umlaut word.

Clip the whole cell that has white space in it and paste and run it again:

  1. Escx to cut the bad cell,
  2. arrow-up one time, and
  3. Escv to paste it after the cell again.

These three shortcuts work so well that I do no longer check whether the cell end position is right. While pasting the cell, the markdown is compiled. Then, the error is gone at once, without leaving and opening the session.

Finding the "bad markup cell"

If you do not check it at once, it may take a long time to find the bad cell, or you need to reopen the notebook. That is why you should check the cells of the neighbourhood right away when the error pops up at first. You may also open the notebook a second time, search for the same search word again, and then find that cell without the help of the the search box in your "broken search box"-notebook.

Quick fix: open the notebook again

In a huge notebook, you do not know where that white space cell is. You need to find it by scrolling or by chance, but you will not have the time for that. That is why it is enough to save, close and open the notebook again, so that you get back the search box. Yet, the search box error will always pop up again during searching, since search will find something in these white boxes or pass them. At best, you just keep your eyes open while working and searching. As soon as you see by chance such a white box again, like the following, you should fix it right away, else you will run into the search box error again.

Workaround: go on without the search box

I often do not want to close my work and lose the variables in memory. I went over to search with my own eyes, without the search box, when this happened in a running project state. This is worth a hint since I was not aware how quickly you can adapt to this. After a while, I knew my code much better. For a short time, this can be done.

================================

Finding out

I found this strange white space by chance:

While the search bar shows this error everywhere, not just when you see this cell, I was still aware that I did not have such two bugs in one go before. They had to be linked. This white space was always at the same point and was likely the reason for the error: roughly since pasting that text, I remember having had this search error once in a while.

Yet, if I run the markdown cell with the white space again, the writing in the white space can be seen again, and there is no special character that can tell why the search error happens:

--clip-grad NORM <----- FROM HERE, THE WHITE SPACE STARTED
Clip gradient norm (default: None, no clipping)

--sched SCHEDULER
LR scheduler (default: "step")

--lr LR
Learning rate, overrides lr-base if set (default: None)

--warmup-lr LR
Warmup learning rate (default: 1e-5)

If I double click to edit the markdown cell, the white space is back, I cannot see or edit the writing after --clip-grad NORM. I cannot even mark any text in the edit mode and therefore cannot clip the text.

My guess: a space sign that is forbidden in markdown. Or something else that makes the text more than a text or a broken text. That would also go along with the Error "TypeError: can't access property "length", child is undefined".

Q: Vue 3 reactivity issue A:

I created a minimal reproduction of the behavior. There is a documents array that is not reactive, and a Recent array that is deeply reactive.

In this case, the allActivities computed value only updates when the reactive Recent.value changes; documents does not trigger a reactive update.

  • Vue SFC Playground

Assuming that only Recent can contain records that can be unchecked, the problem shouldn't occur. The issue can only happen if documents contains records with checked: 0 - which shouldn't be the case. I think at this point you should check the items in documents.

Q: FastAPI backend always returns HTTP 200 on login (even with wrong credentials) and no cookie is set after deployment A:

The issue is in your FastAPI code, not nginx.

This block runs before you validate the credentials:

if request.session and request.session["role"] == "admin":
    response = {"status": "success", "message": "login successful"}
    return JSONResponse(content=response, status_code=200)

request.session always exists once SessionMiddleware is enabled, and in production (behind a proxy) it may already contain session data. As a result, this condition short-circuits the request and returns 200 without checking the username or password.

That’s why you see “authentication successful” for invalid credentials after deployment.

Your frontend and backend are on different subdomains, so this is a cross-site request. Session cookies will be dropped unless:

  • SessionMiddleware is configured with same_site="none" and https_only=True

  • The frontend sends requests with credentials: "include"

If those are missing, the browser silently rejects the cookie, and the session never persists.

Q: Vectorise coincidences lookup between numpy arrays A:

The following code includes the function count_searchsorted(x, y) that computes your result using two applications of np.searchsorted. For N >= 100, it is generally faster than the broadcasting-based implementation in count_broadcasting(x, y). The time complexity of count_searchsorted(x, y) with inputs with lengths N and M is O(log(max(M, N))*min(M, N)).

import numpy as np


def count_searchsorted(x, y):
    if len(x) < len(y):
        x, y = y, x
    q1 = np.searchsorted(x, y - 1, side='left')
    q2 = np.searchsorted(x, y + 1, side='right')
    return np.count_nonzero(q1 != q2)


def count_broadcasting(x, y):
    return np.any(np.abs(x - y[:, np.newaxis]) == 1, axis=1).sum()


def generate_data(N, rng=None):
    """
    Returns two arrays, each with length N.
    Each array is strictly monotonically increasing.
    The smallest difference between two consecutive values in each array is 2.
    The intersection of the two arrays is empty.
    The arrays do not necessarily satisfy all the assumptions given in the
    question, but they have the properties necessary to test the implementations
    in this file.
    """
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng()
    # The following expression assumes N is not very small; we expect N >= 100.
    allowed_gaps = 2 + rng.choice(N // 4, size=N // 2)
    gaps = rng.choice(allowed_gaps, size=N)
    x = np.cumulative_sum(gaps[:-1], include_initial=True) + rng.integers(20)
    incr = rng.integers(0, gaps - 1)
    incr[incr == 0] = -1
    y = x + incr
    return x, y

For example, here's a test with N = M = 100.

Generate some data:

In [211]: N = 100

In [212]: x, y = generate_data(N)

Check that the two functions give the same result:

In [213]: count_broadcasting(x, y)
Out[213]: np.int64(31)

In [214]: count_searchsorted(x, y)
Out[214]: np.int64(31)

Timing:

In [215]: %timeit count_broadcasting(x, y)
12.2 μs ± 210 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100,000 loops each)

In [216]: %timeit count_searchsorted(x, y)
6.99 μs ± 14.2 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100,000 loops each)

So the searchsorted-based function is about 1.75 times faster.

For longer inputs, the difference in performance is more significant:

In [218]: N = 2000

In [219]: x, y = generate_data(N)

In [220]: count_broadcasting(x, y)
Out[220]: np.int64(64)

In [221]: count_searchsorted(x, y)
Out[221]: np.int64(64)

In [222]: %timeit count_broadcasting(x, y)
6.9 ms ± 23.9 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)

In [223]: %timeit count_searchsorted(x, y)
149 μs ± 76.6 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000 loops each)

So with N = M = 2000, the searchsorted-based function is more than 46 times faster.
